commits.message:
[cleanup] Delete unreachable code and centralize profiling defaults (#8761)

Levanter's SSD Pallas backend never existed. `ssd_intra_chunk_pallas`
unconditionally raised `PallasUnsupportedError`, so the `pallas_tpu`
entry in
`IMPLEMENTATIONS`, the warning-dedup cache, the fallback loop over
implementations, and the `ExceptionGroup` path built to recover from
that raise
could never do anything. Backend selection is now a single lookup, and
the
local-block branch in `ssd_chunked_forward` that only the Pallas path
reached is
gone. `BlockSizes` was documented as reserved for that future kernel and
carried
no value any kernel read; it, `interpret`, and `backend` were declared
on eleven
Mamba-3 entrypoints where every terminal consumer discarded them with
`del`. All
three are removed along with `ssd/config.py`. Nothing outside the `ssd`
and
`mamba3` packages referenced them.

`Controller.last_scheduling_context` in iris had no reader. Its
docstring
claimed the dashboard consumed it, but the dashboard calls
`get_job_scheduling_diagnostics`, which is untouched. Every scheduling
tick
stored a full `SchedulingContext` (workers, pending task rows,
capacities) that
nothing read and that stayed alive until the next tick replaced it. The
property, its backing field, and the `ControllerProtocol` member are
removed,
along with the attributes three test doubles set only to satisfy the
protocol.
`ScheduleResult.scheduling_context` stays because the scheduling pass
reads it
for a completion log line.

Zephyr's `shuffle.py` defined `_fan_in_groups` twice back to back with
identical
bodies, so the first was shadowed. The copy-paste came from #8204.

In marin's profiling package, `warmup_steps`, `hot_op_limit`, and
`breakdown_mode` each repeated their default across seven signatures in
`ingest.py`, `xplane.py`, and `cli.py`, and `cli.py` kept its own
`_BREAKDOWN_MODES` tuple of valid modes separate from the dispatch in
`summarize_event_tracks`, so the two could drift. A `BreakdownMode`
StrEnum and
the three defaults now live in `trace_summary.py`, and the CLI derives
its
`--breakdown-mode` choices from the enum. CLI help text and defaults are
unchanged.

Selecting the Mamba-3 kernel tests on their own then exposed a latent
order-dependency. `test_pallas_mamba3.py` compares XLA and reference
kernels at
`atol=rtol=1e-5`, but TPU runs float32 matmuls through lower-precision
passes by
default, leaving a gap near 5e-4. The file passed on TPU only because
`test_gdn_kernels.py` sets `jax_default_matmul_precision` globally at
import
time, so the tolerance held whenever both modules were collected in the
same
session. It now sets that precision itself, matching
`test_gdn_kernels.py` and
`test_gdn_layer.py`.

commits.author: Helw150
commits.message:
[agents] Add maintainability pass to PR review (#8746)

Add a bounded maintainability pass to `review-pr`. It selects at most
four high-impact changes, such as public interfaces, state transitions,
or abstraction boundaries, and assigns one reviewer to each. A reviewer
sees one selected file or cohesive diff hunk and returns at most one
candidate finding. Generated files, formatting, mechanical renames, and
repetitive call-site edits receive no reviewer slot.

Reviewers reason through hypothetical small changes to adjacent behavior
without modifying code or publishing the scenario. This exercise finds
coupling, hidden assumptions, and unnecessary layers that reduce
flexibility. The coordinating reviewer uses the PR description and
broader code context to reject speculative candidates. Published
comments describe the structural obstacle. The rubric favors locally
self-contained implementations that can change without modifying
unrelated variants, including small duplication that preserves
independence. Reviewer roles and finding categories are independent of
the agent provider and model.

Extend the shared writing-style check with short active sentences,
concrete words, stable terms, and explainable jargon. Agents applying
this check omit or research terms whose provenance or exact meaning they
cannot explain. For PR bodies, issues, documentation, and reports,
another agent performs a cold read using only the draft and intended
audience. The author applies the smallest local fix, links long
background, or narrows the claim to avoid information overload.

commits.message:
[codehealth] Automate review enforcement and feedback collection (#8740)

Replace the Claude pull-request jobs with two independent Loom sessions:
one correctness review and one lint-catalog review. The trusted
default-branch workflow accepts only trusted same-repository pull
requests, checks out only the shared launch action from `main`, and
passes the immutable head SHA to each session. The `agentic-lint` label
remains the required proof that an agent completed the local commit
workflow.

Run review-feedback aggregation directly on a daily GitHub runner. The
job uses the existing CI Google and SSH credentials for Finelog and a
repository OpenAI key mirrored from Secret Manager. Classification uses
GPT-5.6 Terra at medium effort in a read-only, schema-constrained Codex
process, with inline diff hunks or bounded pull-request patch context.
GitHub fetch, classification, and Finelog flush failures stop the run.
Bot output and agent comments carrying the required `🤖` marker are
excluded from the human-review denominator.

Loom exposes workload federation and `runs.create` as API-only
operations. A shared composite action calls their canonical REST
endpoints for the pull-request and fork-ferry workflows.

A dry run on #8735 fetched six human comments; the previous path counted
fourteen because it included eight agent replies. The six-comment
classification completed in 16 seconds and identified one generously
catchable comment.

Scheduled report publication remains in the refinement PR. The
refinement results need a durable artifact that can hold benchmark
evidence as well as the rolling metrics.

Part of #8738

commits.message:
[iris] Add generic server-side resource reads (#8675)

Expose internal Get, List, and BatchGet resource verbs for Job, Task,
Attempt, Worker, Endpoint, User, User-budget, Backend, and Peer reads
while keeping all first-party clients on ControllerService. Controller
composition registers protobuf handlers beside their noun
implementations. The only new noun behavior is exact numbered Attempt
lookup and ordered retry history over existing Attempt rows. Generic
dispatch imports no noun schemas, and every binding declares
dashboard-read access.

Both wire surfaces invoke the same controller operations. Verb-specific
registration methods keep decoding and response shaping at the RPC
boundary without a second noun service. Generic responses normalize
single resources, lists with pagination metadata, and ordered batch
snapshots. List codecs may also attach typed noun-owned aggregate
metadata; Backend reads retain the unroutable-job count and sample.
Controllers and local proxies always mount the service, which permits
canary probes without changing CLI, SDK, worker, dashboard, or
federation traffic. The generic contract remains internal and may change
before client cutover.

The local-cluster parity probe passed for completed Job, Task, exact
Attempt, Attempt history, Worker, Backend, and batch Job-state reads.
The diff-driven safe suite passed 4,504 tests.

Part of #7560

commits.author: mcwitt
commits.message:
[grug] Rework the ragged all-to-all expert-parallel MoE backend (#8549)

Reworks the ragged all-to-all expert-parallel MoE backend into a
replacement for the pooled-wave hero transport. In an A/B at the hero
shape — both arms restored from the live hero's step-6000 checkpoint on
real data, one NVL72 rack, transport the only variable — ragged
delivers:

- **matching-to-slightly-ahead throughput**: **22.87 vs 22.71 MFU**,
with the two arms run back to back on the same rack so placement
differences cannot account for the gap (standard deviation across the
scored steps: 0.11 for ragged, 0.59 for pooled-wave; three earlier runs
of the ragged configuration ranged 22.34–22.58)
- **~150× lower drop rate**: **0.018%** vs 2.67% of expert assignments
under the trained router, with the loss at the scored step
correspondingly lower (1.4727 vs 1.4777)
- **~12 GiB lower runtime device peak**: **137.9 vs 149.9 GiB** at
identical steady-state footprint

This PR does not change the default backend: the `moe_hero_ep` entry
points keep `fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all`, and the ragged backend is
opt-in via `moe_implementation="ragged_all_to_all"`.

Key changes:

- **Expert-granular transport data path** — one `ragged_all_to_all`
update per (peer, local expert): senders read each expert group's
accepted prefix in place and rows arrive grouped by expert, replacing
~1.1 s/step of repeat/sort/compact permutes. With chunking, **+1.5 MFU**
over the prior ragged path.
- **Sequential expert chunks** — local experts run in two chunks with
per-chunk capacity, halving the transport buffers XLA cannot
rematerialize. Not a tuning choice: the unchunked graph needs 192–194
GiB against 184 GiB HBM and OOMs at the first hero step.
- **QuACK SM100 grouped GEMMs + cuDNN grouped weight gradients** for the
expert MLP — the core of the earlier **16.1% → 21.9%** stack. Those two
figures were measured before the current protocol and are not directly
comparable to the numbers above. SM100 + SiLU only; everything else
keeps XLA's `ragged_dot`.
- **Device-initiated transport** — the ragged backend engages XLA's
device-initiated (NCCL LSA) ragged-all-to-all kernel through `XLA_FLAGS`
defaults it sets itself. The kernel partitions copy work across CTAs by
bytes, so splitting a peer transfer into several updates buys no load
balance and only adds granularity cost (21.12 MFU when we measured it at
64 splits, against 22.34–22.58 unsplit). The backend therefore exposes
no splitting option, and the two flags are not overridable: the
host-launched kernel would need both flags cleared together plus the
update splitting this backend does not produce, so a partial override
would silently run a configuration nothing here measures.
- **Fused combine gather + weighted sum** and a backend-specific
scheduling posture (latency-hiding scheduler off, collective overlap 1)
— part of the stack above. The scheduler is off for memory, not
scheduling: its longer live ranges fail NCCL's first-step allocations at
the current HBM budget, and a follow-up that offloads layer activations
to pinned host re-enables it at a measured gain (#8317).
- **`--master-params` option** — fp32 weights on device instead of a
pinned-host master: **~+0.4 MFU**.
- **Validation harness** — the 4-GPU `ragged_ep_check` gates forward and
gradients against an exact fp32 dense reference, both at a capacity high
enough that nothing is clipped and in the drop regime the hero actually
trains in. For the latter it computes which assignments survive in NumPy
— accepted rows are the prefix of each expert group under a greedy
first-sender-wins gate, so the surviving set is a pure function of the
routing and the capacity — and requires the transport to equal dense
over exactly the rows it kept. It also records which kernels the run
selected, since that depends on the device and the installed packages.
Nothing runs it on a schedule, and it sits under `experiments/` rather
than `tests/cluster/`, because the repository has no marker, fixture, or
workflow for a test that needs particular accelerators (#8704). That
same gap silences the two unit tests that exercise this backend end to
end: both skip under CI's single CPU device, and `addopts` carries no
`-rs`, so the skips do not appear in the output. Separately, a d768
ablation pair (10.8k steps, identical settings) has ragged ahead of
pooled-wave on train loss (**1.939 vs 1.956**), eval bpb (**0.975 vs
1.033**), and steady-state drop rate (**~0.03% vs ~2.7%** at that
scale).

Context: pooled-wave is the hero default but drops a low-single-digit
percentage of expert assignments at steady state. The goal here is
at-least-parity throughput with materially fewer drops, without touching
the model or precision. That trade matters most for long-context
training, where a batch holds fewer, longer examples: per-shard token
pools average over fewer documents, routing skew grows, and capacity
clipping bites harder. Memory is a second operational motivation. The
hero's intermittent OOMs traced to the step peak overshooting the
cuda_async release threshold (#8490), and main now holds the production
pooled-wave hero under that threshold by shrinking the train-step arena
(#8507, slop factor 85) with the master kept on pinned host. Ragged
reaches the same safety with ~12 GiB to spare: in that same paired run,
where both arms carry the heavier fp32-on-device master, pooled-wave
still peaks 11.7 GiB over the threshold (149.9 vs 138.2 GiB) while
ragged sits just under it (137.9 GiB) — headroom that loosens the arena
and master-placement constraints the pooled posture needs.

Caveat — **quoted throughput depends on an XLA patch, shipped
separately.** The device kernel itself runs on stock XLA (jax ≥ 0.11.1
defines the flags; older jaxlibs abort at import on unknown `XLA_FLAGS`
entries), but its stock CTA assignment starves under trained-router skew
and measures ~19.4% MFU at this shape. The quoted numbers use a
one-commit balanced-CTA-assignment patch,
[mcwitt/xla@d6d3132a90](https://github.com/mcwitt/xla/commit/d6d3132a90dada14d570b66da38eccb7f6d774a3)
(2.35× on the standalone transport benchmark; being upstreamed). This PR
does not ship a wheel; the pinned build lands in a follow-up. The 4-GPU
validation has been run green on GB200 against the host-launched kernel,
which exercises the expert-MLP kernels and the offset arithmetic;
re-running it against the device kernel needs that build.

Part of #8317. Per-arm ledgers and trace anatomy live on
`research/mcwitt/8317-ragged-tune` under
`autoresearch/loop-260821-leg2/` (one-shot tuning) and on
`research/mcwitt/8317-dk-native` under
`autoresearch/loop-260824-dkperf/` (device-kernel root-cause and the
balanced-CTA result).
